newsitem.title: FRANCE: French doctors' strike widens, govt stands firm.
newsitem.headline: French doctors' strike widens, govt stands firm.

text.p: French junior hospital doctors angry over health reform plans hardened their strike movement on Wednesday, vowing to prolong the protest as the government accused them of acting out of self-interest.
Doctors' disruption of routine medical activities spread to 22 of 26 French cities with teaching hospitals. Emergency care at all hospitals is guaranteed by law.

Challenging the conservative government's plans to brake health spending, the strikers are demanding withdrawal of measures to punish doctors who overspend, and a renegotiation of administrative agreements regulating their activities.
The government has vowed not to yield to their demands.

It can ill afford to let the strikers win since reducing France's health fund deficit is a key part of French efforts to qualify for a planned single European currency, set to start on January 1, 1999.

"We are not going to let ourselves be hindered by what is no longer a love of medicine, but is born of worries that are too self-interested," Labour Minister Jacques Barrot said before leaving for the northern town of Amiens to meet strikers.
By Wednesday the junior practitioners, who are supported by unions representing specialist doctors in private practice, had been joined by some senior medical staff at hospitals.
"The movement covers all junior doctors, hospital personnel, hospital doctors and even social security beneficiaries," said a union delegate.
France's largest medical union, the general practitioners' MG France, opposes the strike and supports the reform plan.
The strike was sparked on March 11 by plans to fine doctors who overshoot government-set limits on medical costs.
Strikers plan to march through Paris from Bastille Square on Thursday, flanked by specialist doctors.

On Tuesday Prime Minister Alain Juppe assigned 37 parliamentarians of the centre-right ruling coalition to fan out across the country to explain the government's plan to hospital doctors and staff. Several set off on Wednesday to begin their task.
Public health care spending is the leading factor in France's welfare deficit, expected to show a shortfall of about 33 billion francs ($5.8 billion) this year after 51.6 billion francs last year.
The specialist doctors' unions say the changes will make them pay between 6,000 and 100,000 francs if national health costs go over budget in 1997.
The plan challenges what was previously the almost total freedom of French doctors to consult and prescribe as they wish.
The state health insurance plan, to which the vast majority of the population belongs, reimburses patients partially for any medicine, test or procedure prescribed.
